newsitem.title: USA: US stocks to open lower on FOMC meeting, holidays.
newsitem.headline: US stocks to open lower on FOMC meeting, holidays.

text.p: Wall Street stocks should open slightly lower in thin trading on Monday, held in check until investors know more about the outcome of tomorrow's Fed meeting and by Jewish and Japanese holidays.

"It should be a dull session with a slightly downside bias," said Prudential securities market analyst Hildegard Zagorski. "The market should stay in a holding pattern ... I don't see anyone getting rambunctious before the Fed meeting."
Tuesday, the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will hold a meeting on interest rate policy.
The long bond was off 7/32 to yield 7.06 percent and Standard & Poor's December futures were off 2.5 to 689.4.

Westfalia Investments director of research Peter Cardillo said, "We should see a lower opening on very slow volume with some profit-taking and squaring of positions as we head into the FOMC meeting .. Technically, we're in a strong position. A 25 basis point rise in interest rates would probably further expand the bullish posture the market is already in."
Cardillo noted that today's Yom Kippur Jewish holiday as well as a the Japanese national holiday celebrating the first day of fall would also dampen markets.
The Japanese market was closed for the national holiday.

One chance for strength in the market today could be the dollar, Cardillo said. "If it strengthens against the European currencies due to the latest Yeltsin reports, there's an outside chance it could push the market."
Doubts about the health of Russian President Boris Yeltsin have hurt Russian bonds and funds.
The dollar was stuck in ranges in a quiet European session.

In London, the key FTSE-100 index fell almost 40 to 3925. U.S. stocks were trading mostly weaker in London ahead of the Fed meeting, although oil stocks continued to firm on expectations that demand will outpace supplies.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed Friday up 21 to about 5888.
The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column says Salomon Inc investors are concerned about Warren Buffett's plan to shed just under a half of his 18 percent stake in Salomon.
The New York Times says Time Warner Inc's combination with Tuner Broadcasting could give Time Warner stock a chance to boost itself after six and a half years of lethargy.
